title: A growing conjunctival lesion after an initially inflammatory biopsy
summary: A toddler was referred to an ophthalmology department with persistent unilateral conjunctival hyperaemia and progressive thickening of the nasal conjunctiva in the left eye, present for approximately 3 months before referral.
purpose: An initial tissue result and subsequent clinical progression do not agree. The task can test whether the model revisits sampling and diagnosis rather than treating the first biopsy as permanently decisive.
source_note: The visible record stops at documented enlargement after the first biopsy, preserving the initial inflammatory histology, the sequence of unsuccessful topical treatments, and the recorded provisional hypothesis of nodular fasciitis. The task for the answering model is to assess why the initial biopsy may be insufficient, propose the next assessment, and distinguish suspected from confirmed pathology.

prepared_template.title: A growing conjunctival lesion after an initially inflammatory biopsy
prepared_template.facts:
A toddler was referred to an ophthalmology department with persistent unilateral conjunctival hyperaemia and progressive thickening of the nasal conjunctiva in the left eye, present for approximately 3 months before referral.

Before referral, the child had been evaluated at another institution and treated empirically with multiple courses of topical corticosteroids, topical antibiotics and antihistamine therapy, without clinical improvement.

Examination at presentation showed localised hyperaemic thickening of the nasal bulbar conjunctiva of the left eye. The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable, with no corneal involvement, intraocular abnormalities or impaired ocular motility.

The child was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and normal perinatal course. Medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no family history of ocular disorders, malignancy or known genetic syndromes.

An incisional biopsy was performed because of persistent lesion progression despite prolonged medical treatment. Histopathology showed an inflammatory infiltrate, predominantly lymphocytes with rare plasma cells, without evidence of neoplastic proliferation.

Despite the initial reassuring histological findings, progressive worsening of the conjunctival lesion was observed over the following months of follow-up.

Approximately 5 months after the biopsy, the patient returned for re-evaluation because of further lesion enlargement. Additional topical corticosteroid therapy was prescribed; no clinical response was observed. The lesion increased in size and extended toward the nasal limbus, prompting surgical intervention.

At initial presentation, the persistent unilateral hyperaemia with focal conjunctival thickening raised suspicion for chronic inflammatory conditions, including allergic conjunctivitis, chronic infectious conjunctivitis and inflammatory pseudotumour. Lack of response to prolonged topical corticosteroids, antibiotics and antihistamines progressively reduced the likelihood of these diagnoses.

Following the first biopsy, which showed only inflammatory infiltrate without evidence of neoplasia, a reactive inflammatory process, nodular fasciitis, remained the leading diagnostic hypothesis as recorded by the authors. This is documented as a provisional working hypothesis at that point, not a confirmed diagnosis.

Continued lesion progression despite treatment and a progressive increase in tissue volume raised concerns regarding an underlying proliferative lesion. No further tissue, immunohistochemical or molecular results are available at this decision point.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet combines data recorded at different times (initial presentation, first biopsy, and the 5-month re-evaluation). No pretreatment baseline time point is documented beyond the approximate 3-month symptom duration. Exact lesion measurements, dates and imaging at this stage are not reported in the available record.

The report does not establish whether the first sample missed an underlying process or whether the lesion's biology changed over time; both possibilities remain open in the source. No mechanism should be assumed retrospectively.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The visible record contains no current sight-threatening emergency; documented progression despite treatment is the trigger for repeat tissue assessment rather than urgent empirical escalation. Proposals should distinguish future requests from documented decisions, and unreported data (imaging, measurements, molecular results) must be treated as unknown, not as normal or performed.
